def_a: A multicoloured arch in the sky, produced by prismatic refraction of light within droplets of rain in the air.

etym_text_b: From Old Norse regnbogi (“rainbow”), from Proto-Germanic *regnabugô.

def_a: A country in Southern Africa. Official name: Kingdom of Lesotho. Capital: Maseru.

etym_text_b:
Internationalism, based on Sotho Lesotho (“land of the Basotho (Sotho people)”). The immediate transmission route into Norwegian is unknown.
The Sotho name belongs to a characteristic noun-class pattern based on Sotho: Mosotho (“a Sotho person”), Basotho (“Sotho people”), Sesotho (“Sotho language”) and Lesotho (“land of the Basotho”).
Parallel international adaptations include Norwegian Nynorsk Lesotho, Afrikaans Lesotho, Swedish Lesotho, German Lesotho, Dutch Lesotho and English Lesotho.

etym_text_a:
From Middle High German sæjen, from Old High German sāen, sājen, sāwen, from Proto-West Germanic *sāan, from Proto-Germanic *sēaną, from Proto-Indo-European *seh₁-.
Compare Dutch zaaien, English sow, Danish så, Gothic 𐍃𐌰𐌹𐌰𐌽 (saian). The expected modern spelling would be with an -h- to mark the hiatus (as in mähen, nähen), but this was avoided to distinguish säen from sähen, subjunctive of sehen (“to see”).

Alternative etymology derives hurry as a variant of harry.

def_a: An Old Norse (Icelandic) prose narrative, especially one dealing with family or social histories and legends.
etym_text_a:
From Old Norse saga (“epic tale, story”), from Proto-Germanic *sagǭ (“saying, story”), from Proto-Indo-European *sekʷ- (“to say”).
Cognate with Old English sagu (“story, tale, statement”), Old High German saga (“an assertion, narrative, sermon, pronouncement”), Icelandic saga (“story, tale, history”), German Sage (“saga, legend, myth”). More at say; Doublet of saw.
Compare typologically Ancient Greek ἔπος (épos) (whence epos, epic) << Proto-Indo-European *wekʷ- (“to speak”).
etym_text_b:
From Old Swedish sagha, from Old Norse saga, from Proto-Germanic *sagǭ. First attested in the mid-14th century
Cognate with Danish saghæ, Jutish save (“a narrative, a narration, a tale, a report”), Norwegian Nynorsk soge, Faroese søga, Icelandic saga, German Sage, English saw. Perhaps related to Lithuanian pasaka.

def_a: To propel oneself rapidly upward, downward and/or in any horizontal direction such that momentum causes the body to become airborne.

etym_text_a:
From Middle English jumpen (“to walk quickly, run, jump”), probably of Middle Low German or North Germanic origin, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *gumpōną ~ *gumbōną (“to hop, skip, bounce”), an iterative verb. The OED suggests an imitative origin. Related to jumble. In the sense “to propel oneself” it displaced leap partially and spring largely.
Cognates
Cognate with German Low German jumpen (“to jump”), archaic German gumpen (“to jump, hop, bounce”), dialectal German gampen (“to hop”), Alemann
etym_text_b: From Old Norse hoppa.

etym_text_a:

def_a: Traditionally the fourth of the four seasons, typically regarded as spanning either the period between the winter solstice to the spring equinox, or the months of December, January, and February in temperate and polar regions of the Northern Hemisphere and the months of June, July, and August in the Southern Hemisphere. It is the time when the sun is lowest in the sky, resulting in short days, and the time of year with the lowest atmospheric temperatures for the region.

def_a: Having a thick edge or point; not sharp.

From Middle English blunt, blont, from Old English *blunt, probably of North Germanic origin, possibly related to Old Norse blunda (“to shut eyes, to doze”), related to blind (> Icelandic blunda, Swedish blunda, Danish blunde).
Compare the Scandinavian-German munitons term blind (“non-live, dummy”), opposite of skarp (“live”, literally, “sharp”): Swedish and Danish blind patron (“dummy round”), Danish blindt skud, German blinder schuss (“dummy shot”), blinde granate (“dummy grenade”).

From Middle English blunt, blont, from Old English *blunt, probably of North Germanic origin, possibly related to Old Norse blunda (“to shut eyes, to doze”), related to blind (> Icelandic blunda, Swedish blunda, Danish blunde).
Compare the Scandinavian-German munitons term blind (“non-live, dummy”), opposite of skarp (“live”, literally, “sharp”): Swedish and Danish blind patron (“dummy round”), Danish blindt skud, German blinder schuss (“dummy shot”), blinde granate (“dummy grenade”).

Internationalism, based on Latin Iuppiter (“Jupiter, the chief Roman god”), also Iūpiter. The Latin nominative continues an ancient vocative expression combining the name of the sky god with pater (“father”), essentially “Father Jove”; compare the oblique stem Iov-, seen in the genitive Iovis.
The name continues Proto-Italic *djous patēr (“sky father”), from *djous (“day, sky”) + *patēr (“father”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *dyḗws (“sky; sky god”) and *ph₂tḗr (“father”). The first elem
senses_b.gloss: Jupiter; the chief Roman god, ruler of the sky and weather and especially associated with thunder and lightning, corresponding to the Greek god Zeus

senses_b.etym_text:
Borrowed from English Jupiter (“Jupiter, Florida”). The place name has a distinct history from the directly mythological and astronomical senses above. According to the official history of the Town of Jupiter, Spanish maps of the area showed the local river as Rio Jobe, the second element apparently referring to the indigenous Jobe people who inhabited the area.
After Britain acquired Florida from Spain in 1763, British mapmakers encountered the name Jobe and reinterpreted or Anglicized it as Jo

senses_b.etym_text:
Borrowed from Romanian Jupiter (“Jupiter, Romanian seaside resort”), itself named after Jupiter (“Jupiter, the planet”).
The resort was created during the large-scale development of Romania's southern Black Sea coast in the late 1960s and early 1970s. It belongs to a deliberately astronomical series of neighbouring resort names which includes Neptun, Venus and Saturn, all named after planets; Romanian sources commonly refer to these resorts collectively as the “planets” of the coast.

def_b: a wire, a rope, a line
etym_text_a: From Middle High German lint, linde, from Old High German lind, lindi, from Proto-West Germanic *linþ(ī), from Proto-Germanic *linþaz. Cognate with English lithe.
etym_text_b:
From Old Norse lína, from Proto-Germanic *līnǭ (“line, rope, flaxen cord, thread”), from *līną (“flax”).
Hypothetised to be derived from Proto-Indo-European *līno- (“flax”), although it's impossible to reconstruct a common PIE protoform due to discrepancies with other European branches and absence of cognates outside of Europe.
If originally a non-IE loanword, locating the source is impossible because cultivation of linen was widespread in the region since the Neolithic.

def_b: The fifth day of the week in many religious traditions, and the fourth day of the week in systems using the ISO 8601 norm; it follows Wednesday and precedes Friday.
etym_text_a: From Middle High German donerstac, from Old High German donarestag, thonarestag (11th c.), from Proto-West Germanic *Þunras dag (“day of the thunder god”). Compare Bavarian Dunnersdåg, Low German Dunnersdag, Dutch donderdag, West Frisian tongersdei, English Thursday, Danish torsdag.
etym_text_b:
From Middle English Thursday, Thuresday, from Old English þursdæġ, þuresdæġ (“Thursday”), possibly from a contraction of þunresdæġ (“Thursday”, literally “Thor's day”), or of North Germanic origin, from Old Norse þórsdagr; all from Proto-West Germanic *Þunras dag (“day of the thunder god”). Compare West Frisian tongersdei, German Low German Dunnersdag, Dutch donderdag, German Donnerstag, Danish torsdag. More at thunder, day.
